verdicts.why: A plain body-part name; it takes no side on anything it is aimed at.
'The critical eye', 'in their eyes' name attention or viewpoint plainly; any judgement in the sentences comes from the surrounding words, not from 'eye'.
A neutral spatial term (the eye of a storm); nothing to warn a learner about.
The hole in a needle; purely descriptive.
It names the speaker's own pleasure, which is its meaning, not an attitude laid on top of it; it is the plain word beside 'happy' and 'pleased'.
'Glad to help' states willingness; it is the ordinary, unmarked way to say so and judges nothing.
The 'should avoid' framing is the sense itself, not a tone beyond it, and the sentences use it as the plain word for an inducement one might resist.
A degree word ('half alive', 'half finished'); it measures and does not judge.
A more formal register than 'talk' but no attitude toward the talkers or the talk; register is not judgement.
A neutral measure word; the degree it names is whatever the sentence says it is.
A plain word for area or reach ('a wide extent'); nothing evaluative in it.
A literary word for 'hurry'; the sentences show no scorn or approval of the hurrier, only speed.
Acting quickly is the whole meaning; it does not colour the actor.
'Hastened his journey' says something was sped up, with no side taken on whether that was good.
'Hastening to the same vexatious conclusion' is disliked because of 'vexatious', not because of 'hasten', which is neutral about outcomes.
An unpleasant referent named by the plainest available word; 'hurt feelings' is the neutral baseline against which 'wound' or 'sting' would be the marked choices.
Naming emotional pain is the meaning; the word carries no attitude toward the sufferer or the cause.
Bad referent, plain word; it is what 'harm' and 'injure' are measured against, not a coloured alternative to them.
'This hurts' states a fact about pain; nothing beyond the meaning.
Damage is a bad thing, but the word is the flat everyday name for it and takes no side.
Being in pain is a state, plainly named; no judgement rides on the word.

Chosen over 'bad' or 'disastrous', it softens: it expresses polite regret and lays the fault on luck rather than on anyone, so 'a most unfortunate affair' is a well-bred understatement a learner should recognise as such.
Pressing an argument or a course of action earnestly is the meaning; the word approves or scorns neither the urger nor the thing urged.
Impelling in a direction is a plain description of force, with no attitude toward it.
Spurring on with cheers is descriptive of the act; nothing here judges the target.
